function.name: cronjob
function.description:
Manage scheduled cron jobs with a single compressed tool.

Use action='create' to schedule a new job from a prompt or one or more skills.
Use action='list' to inspect jobs.
Use action='update', 'pause', 'resume', 'remove', or 'run' to manage an existing job.

To stop a job the user no longer wants: first action='list' to find the job_id, then action='remove' with that job_id. Never guess job IDs — always list first.

Jobs run in a fresh session with no current-chat context, so prompts must be self-contained.
If skills are provided on create, the future cron run loads those skills in order, then follows the prompt as the task instruction.
On update, passing skills=[] clears attached skills.

NOTE: The agent's final response is auto-delivered to the target. Put the primary
user-facing content in the final response. Cron jobs run autonomously with no user
present — they cannot ask questions or request clarification.

Important safety rule: cron-run sessions should not recursively schedule more cron jobs.

action.description: One of: create, list, update, pause, resume, remove, run

prompt.description: For create: the full self-contained prompt. If skills are also provided, this becomes the task instruction paired with those skills.

repeat.description: Optional repeat count. Omit for defaults (once for one-shot, forever for recurring).

deliver.description: Omit this parameter to auto-deliver back to the current chat and topic (recommended). Auto-detection preserves thread/topic context. Only set explicitly when the user asks to deliver somewhere OTHER than the current conversation. Values: 'origin' (same as omitting), 'local' (no delivery, save only), or platform:chat_id:thread_id for a specific destination. Examples: 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:#engineering', 'sms:+15551234567'. WARNING: 'platform:chat_id' without :thread_id loses topic targeting.

skills.description: Optional ordered list of skill names to load before executing the cron prompt. On update, pass an empty array to clear attached skills.

model.description: Optional per-job model override. If provider is omitted, the current main provider is pinned at creation time so the job stays stable.

provider.description: Provider name (e.g. 'openrouter', 'anthropic'). Omit to use and pin the current provider.

script.description: Optional path to a Python script that runs before each cron job execution. Its stdout is injected into the prompt as context. Use for data collection and change detection. Relative paths resolve under ~/.hermes/scripts/. On update, pass empty string to clear.

context_from.description: Optional job ID or list of job IDs whose most recent completed output is injected into the prompt as context before each run. Use this to chain cron jobs: job A collects data, job B processes it. Each entry must be a valid job ID (from cronjob action='list'). Note: injects the most recent completed output — does not wait for upstream jobs running in the same tick. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

enabled_toolsets.description: Optional list of toolset names to restrict the job's agent to (e.g. ["web", "terminal", "file", "delegation"]). When set, only tools from these toolsets are loaded, significantly reducing input token overhead. When omitted, all default tools are loaded. Infer from the job's prompt — e.g. use "web" if it calls web_search, "terminal" if it runs scripts, "file" if it reads files, "delegation" if it calls delegate_task. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

workdir.description: Optional absolute path to run the job from. When set, AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules from that directory are injected into the system prompt, and the terminal/file/code_exec tools use it as their working directory — useful for running a job inside a specific project repo. Must be an absolute path that exists. When unset (default), preserves the original behaviour: no project context files, tools use the scheduler's cwd. On update, pass an empty string to clear. Jobs with workdir run sequentially (not parallel) to keep per-job directories isolated.

Examples: 'telegram', 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:999888777:555444333', 'discord:#bot-home', 'slack:#engineering', 'signal:+155****4567', 'matrix:!roomid:server.org', 'matrix:@user:server.org'

function.name: session_search
function.description:
Search your long-term memory of past conversations, or browse recent sessions. This is your recall -- every past session is searchable, and this tool summarizes what happened.

TWO MODES:
1. Recent sessions (no query): Call with no arguments to see what was worked on recently. Returns titles, previews, and timestamps. Zero LLM cost, instant. Start here when the user asks what were we working on or what did we do recently.
2. Keyword search (with query): Search for specific topics across all past sessions. Returns LLM-generated summaries of matching sessions.

USE THIS PROACTIVELY when:
- The user says 'we did this before', 'remember when', 'last time', 'as I mentioned'
- The user asks about a topic you worked on before but don't have in current context
- The user references a project, person, or concept that seems familiar but isn't in memory
- You want to check if you've solved a similar problem before
- The user asks 'what did we do about X?' or 'how did we fix Y?'

Don't hesitate to search when it is actually cross-session -- it's fast and cheap. Better to search and confirm than to guess or ask the user to repeat themselves.

Search syntax: keywords joined with OR for broad recall (elevenlabs OR baseten OR funding), phrases for exact match ("docker networking"), boolean (python NOT java), prefix (deploy*). IMPORTANT: Use OR between keywords for best results — FTS5 defaults to AND which misses sessions that only mention some terms. If a broad OR query returns nothing, try individual keyword searches in parallel. Returns summaries of the top matching sessions.

query.description: Search query — keywords, phrases, or boolean expressions to find in past sessions. Omit this parameter entirely to browse recent sessions instead (returns titles, previews, timestamps with no LLM cost).

role_filter.description: Optional: only search messages from specific roles (comma-separated). E.g. 'user,assistant' to skip tool outputs.

function.name: skill_manage
function.description:
Manage skills (create, update, delete). Skills are your procedural memory — reusable approaches for recurring task types. New skills go to ~/.hermes/skills/; existing skills can be modified wherever they live.

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'patch'). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: For 'patch': replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false).

category.description: Optional category/domain for organizing the skill (e.g., 'devops', 'data-science', 'mlops'). Creates a subdirectory grouping. Only used with 'create'.

file_path.description: Path to a supporting file within the skill directory. For 'write_file'/'remove_file': required, must be under references/, templates/, scripts/, or assets/. For 'patch': optional, defaults to SKILL.md if omitted.

file_content.description: Content for the file. Required for 'write_file'.

function.name: skill_view
function.description: Skills allow for loading information about specific tasks and workflows, as well as scripts and templates. Load a skill's full content or access its linked files (references, templates, scripts). First call returns SKILL.md content plus a 'linked_files' dict showing available references/templates/scripts. To access those, call again with file_path parameter.

name.description: The skill name (use skills_list to see available skills). For plugin-provided skills, use the qualified form 'plugin:skill' (e.g. 'superpowers:writing-plans').

file_path.description: OPTIONAL: Path to a linked file within the skill (e.g., 'references/api.md', 'templates/config.yaml', 'scripts/validate.py'). Omit to get the main SKILL.md content.

function.name: skills_list
function.description: List available skills (name + description). Use skill_view(name) to load full content.

category.description: Optional category filter to narrow results

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

function.name: text_to_speech

function.name: todo

Manage your task list for the current session. Use for complex tasks with 3+ steps or when the user provides multiple tasks. Call with no parameters to read the current list.

     2|
     3|The convoy crawled into the airlock bay at 1417 hours local time, twelve hours earlier than scheduled. Nobody cheered. The hatches opened and the crew came out moving like people who had been holding bad news too long.
     4|
     5|Gabriel watched them from the inner door of the pressure tunnel. Imani was last out of the lead rover. She pulled her helmet off and stood there with her eyes closed, not saying anything, just breathing recycled air that smelled like other people's sweat and machine oil. That told him everything.
     6|
     7|The drill team had left at dawn the previous day with four rovers, two heavy drills, a melting rig, and seven people. They came back with three rovers—one had thrown a traction belt on bad ground and they'd abandoned it—one drill core in a sample tube that should have been full of ice, and a silence that spread through the base faster than any announcement.
     8|
     9|Jonah was the first to speak. He had come up from the workshop crusted with cutting fluid and metal dust, and he stood at the edge of the staging area with his arms crossed, reading the body language of the returning crew like a fault code.
    10|
    11|"That's it?" he said. "One tube?"
    12|
    13|Imani opened her eyes. "That's what came up."
    14|
    15|"Fourteen hours of drilling, two hundred kilometers of driving, and you brought back a sample you could fit in your pocket."
    16|
    17|"I know what we brought back, Jonah."
    18|
    19|"Then tell me what happened."
    20|
    21|The staging area went quiet. People stopped and turned. Gabriel felt the familiar tension—the kind that came when tired people needed someone to blame.
    22|
    23|Imani set her helmet on the rover hood with deliberate care. "The ground signatures looked right. Every spectral pass before departure showed consistent hydrogen returns. TIR anomaly matched what we'd expect from a shallow ice lens. We drilled to fifteen meters and pulled nothing but dry regolith with trace hydration. Secondary target, twenty-two meters, same result. The tool returns looked like ice. They felt like ice. But the ground didn't deliver."
    24|
    25|"The ground doesn't lie," Jonah said.
    26|
    27|"The ground tells the truth in a language we're still learning to read." Imani's voice was flat. Controlled. "We read the phonetics wrong."
    28|
    29|Mei stepped forward from the crowd gathered at the mess entrance. "What was the actual water content?"
    30|
    31|"On the primary core? 0.4 percent by mass. Bound hydration. Not extractable with our current energy budget without cooking the entire column."
    32|
    33|"Then we can't use it."
    34|
    35|"No shit," Jonah said. "That's the point. We burned seventy hours of collective EVA time, wrote off a rover we can't replace, consumed power we don't have to spare, and came back with a geological curiosity." He turned and pointed a finger at the ceiling, which was the direction of the surface. "We landed in the wrong place."
    36|
    37|"Aldrin chose this site," Elena said.
    38|
    39|She had entered from Command without anyone noticing. She stood in the shadow of the structural column near the rear pressure door, arms at her sides, voice calm in a way that made people pay attention precisely because it was so measured.
    40|
    41|"Aldrin chose it based on the best remote sensing data available from orbital reconnaissance," she continued. "Every survey, every lander mission, every radar pass for thirty years pointed to this region as the most water-rich landing zone in the northern lowlands. The decision wasn't a guess. It was the product of every space agency on Earth."
    42|
    43|"Then Earth was wrong," Jonah said.
    44|
    45|"Earth was working with satellite data from Mars orbit." Imani's voice carried an edge now. "Satellites see the top meter. Sometimes two, if the ground is dry enough. We're looking for ice at ten, fifteen, thirty meters. That's not a measurement error. That's a limitation of the whole approach."
    46|
    47|"So what's your excuse?"
    48|
    49|"I'm not making an excuse. I'm telling you what the science says. The hydrogen returns were real. The thermal signatures were real. But the interpretation was wrong. We thought it meant massive shallow ice. It meant trace hydration in a deep dry layer with a false thermal profile. The data didn't lie—we just read it wrong."
    50|
    51|Gabriel watched Elena's face. She was letting the argument run because she needed to see who would fracture first. That was how she worked. She didn't step into every fire. Sometimes she let the fire expose the weak points in the crew and only then brought the extinguisher.
    52|
    53|The weak points were showing.
    54|
    55|Hiroshi, the youngest of the drill crew, sat on a supply crate with his head down. He had been on Mars for three months and he looked like a man who had just realized the planet was bigger than his training. A woman from Life Support—Gabriel thought her name was Chen—stood near the greenhouse entrance with her arms wrapped around herself, the universal posture of someone who had done the math on how long the base could last without new water.
    56|
    57|Elena let it run another fifteen seconds. Then she stepped into the center of the staging area.
    58|
    59|"Enough."
    60|
    61|She didn't shout. The word carried anyway.
    62|
    63|"We are not having the 'wrong landing site' conversation. That's not a decision tree with useful branches. We're here. The ships are here. The equipment is here. The only question that matters is what we do from this position."
    64|
    65|"We need water," Jonah said.
    66|
    67|"I'm aware of what we need."
    68|
    69|"Then don't tell me we're not—"
    70|
    71|"I'm not telling you anything except what's productive." Elena's voice hardened. "Blame doesn't extract ice. Recrimination doesn't fill a single tank. I've seen exactly what happens to small teams under pressure when they start eating each other, and it doesn't end with more water. It ends with people making worse decisions because they're too busy being right at each other to be right about the problem."
    72|
    73|She turned to Imani. "What's your assessment?"
    74|
    75|"The site we chose has ice. Just not accessible ice. The bound water is real but uneconomical. We'd spend more energy extracting it than we'd recover, which makes the whole exercise thermodynamically stupid. But this region has more varied terrain than our initial surveys covered.     76|
    77|"Priorities were wrong."
    78|

    80|
    81|"Range?"

    85|"Possibly?"
    86|

   208|
   209|"Oxygen," Arun said.

   212|

   214|

   222|

   235|"I've been drawing it. Since about twenty-two hundred hours."
   236|
   237|"Draw it for me now."

   239|Jonah pulled up his tablet and walked her through the design. He did it without jargon, the way he always did. Compressors. Filters. Heat. Ceramic stack. Oxygen collection.    240|
   241|"Seventeen kilowatts continuous," she said finally.
   242|
   243|"Yes."
   244|
   245|"That's not a small ask."
   246|

   252|
   253|Elena looked at him. Her eyes were red at the edges. She had been sleeping in shifts, like everyone else. But her voice was steady.
   254|

   256|
   257|Arun hesitated. That was the question he had been avoiding all night.
   258|
   259|"I'm confident the chemistry works," he said. "Solid oxide electrolysis is proven technology. The Martian atmosphere is consistent. The compressor geometry is straightforward."

   262|
   263|"But nobody has ever built a six-hundred-cell stack in a machine shop on another planet. The thermal gradients during warmup could crack the ceramics.    264|
   265|Elena turned to Jonah. "What's your gut say?"
   266|
   267|Jonah did not look away. "We can build it. The question is whether we'll get the first thermal cycle right. If we do, it runs. If we don't, we crack cells and start over. We have enough ceramic stock for two stacks. Maybe three if we're careful with the offcuts."

   269|"Two shots," Elena said.
   270|
   271|"Two shots."

   282|
   283|"I want Arun on thermal modeling full-time. No other duties until the stack design is locked."
   284|

   293|Jonah and Arun left the command module together. The corridor was dim, lit only by emergency strips. The base was on night cycle. Most of the crew was asleep.

   296|
   297|"I know."
   298|
   299|"If this fails, we don't just lose the power. We lose the confidence that we can solve our own problems. That's harder to replace than a ceramic stack."

   303|"Then we don't fail."

   309|"Seventy-two days," he said.

    10|
    11|## Chapter 1 — The Descent Window
    12|
    13|*Mission AI: "The dust storm is covering the reactor's heat radiators, forcing the Sterling generator offline. I recommend shedding non‑critical loads."*
    14|*Dr. Arun Patel: "Acknowledged. Initiating shutdown."*
    15|
    16|The hull of the Ares‑One shuddered as the first tendrils of Martian atmosphere slapped against its heat shield. Plasma ribbons licked the viewports, turning the forward cameras into a blinding white wash. Commander Elena Varga gripped her restraints, voice steady over the intercom: "Descent profile nominal. Keep your eyes on the altimeter, Arun."
    17|
    18|Below them, through a gap in the plasma, Mars revealed itself — not as the rust‑red postcard of imagination, but as something harder and more honest. A plain of ochre dust stretched toward a jagged horizon. Thin wisps of atmosphere curled around debris that had been accumulating for millions of years. Nothing green. Nothing alive. The barometric readout on Elena's cuff climbed: 12 millibars and falling, drawing the crew deeper into a pressure that wanted nothing to do with human lungs.
    19|
    20|Arun's hands moved across his console without needing to look. Fifteen years of training, four simulation runs this morning alone, and now the numbers dancing at the edge of survivability: peak heating at 1,850 kelvin, dynamic pressure spiking to 1.2 bar, structural loads creeping toward 1.15 gees. He muted the proximity alarm — it had been screaming for the last four minutes — and leaned into his microphone.
    21|
    22|"We are being squeezed, shaken, and cooked all at once," he said, his tone calm but carrying the weight of everything that could go wrong. "Hold on to something."
    23|
    24|Ship Two broke through the plasma first. Its beacon flashed green on Elena's display — steady, assured, alive. A surge of relief cracked through her discipline. Then Ship Three appeared, tilted at a wicked fifteen degrees, one landing strut buried past its ankle joint in fine sediment. Its beacon flickered amber. Status: compromised but standing.
    25|
    26|The descent engine on Ares‑One fired its final correction burn. Elena watched the thrust meter climb and fall in a controlled plume, dust erupting outward in a silent bloom as the lander kissed the surface with a grinding shriek of contact. The landing legs compressed. The frame shuddered. A chunk of thermal tile, shed somewhere in the upper atmosphere, spun away into the haze.
    27|
    28|Inside, the crew flinched. Then silence. Then the pressure seal beeped its confirmation: 101.3 kilopascals and holding.
    29|
    30|Elena allowed herself a tight smile. "Pressure integrity confirmed," she said. "Nobody open anything yet."
    31|
    32|Arun was already running his post‑landing diagnostics. Primary power: nominal — solar arrays had deployed and were feeding the bus. Life support: green across all habitats. The nuclear reactor's containment showed no breach. The Sterling generator, the backup that would keep them alive when the dust stole the sun, was cycling into standby mode exactly as Mission AI had sequenced. He allowed himself a slow exhale.
    33|
    34|"Mission AI, confirm overall status," he said.
    35|
    36|Mission AI's voice filled the cabin — soft, resonant, carrying the particular calm of a mind that had never known a heartbeat. "Ares‑One surface operation confirmed. Structural integrity: acceptable. Life support: fully operational. Power bus: solar primary, Sterling on standby. I am monitoring reactor coolant flow and tracking a regional dust front to the east. All crew physiology: nominal. Welcome to Mars, Arun."
    37|
    38|Arun allowed himself a quiet laugh. Fifteen years working with Mission AI, and it still sounded like it meant every word.
    39|
    40|Through the viewscreen — still smeared with descent residue — Elena watched the other two ships in the fading daylight. Ship Two sat level on the plain, its beacon steady green. Ship Three listed badly, its tilt visible even at this distance. Dust continued to drift across the site in long parallel waves, the product of winds that had been sculpting this landscape for millions of years without a single living witness.
    41|
    42|She unstrapped and floated to the comm station. Gabriel Winter was already there, his tablet recording everything.
    43|
    44|"They look less like explorers," Gabriel murmured, half to himself. "And more like survivors already."
    45|
    46|Elena studied the scene without responding immediately. Three ships on a plain. Thirty souls between them. Enough equipment to build something, maybe, if nothing catastrophic went wrong in the next seventy-two hours. She thought of the cargo manifests she had memorized on the transit: 160 metric tons of equipment, supplies, and infrastructure. Pressurized habitats. Water extraction units. Greenhouse modules. A nuclear reactor and its shielding. Enough spare parts to keep a small city running for two years — if it stayed small.
    47|
    48|And it would. She understood that now in a way she hadn't when the mission was approved. This was not a staging ground for a return. This was a beginning.
    49|
    50|"The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact," Gabriel said, still recording.
    51|
    52|"Then let's go find out if we won," Elena said, and reached for the hatch release.
    53|
    54|Outside, the wind carried the faint tick of settling dust against the hull. The sky was the color of a bruised peach, darkening toward black at the zenith. Somewhere beyond the horizon, a dust storm was building — Mission AI had been tracking it for six hours — but it was moving slowly and trending south. For now, the eastern sky held a thin ribbon of pink light.
    55|
    56|Elena stood at the base of the ladder, looking up at the three ships, her breath fogging inside her helmet. The cold was already seeping through the suit insulation, a dry cold that felt like sandpaper on exposed skin. She thought about what Mission AI had said about the dust storm — nine days before it reached them, maybe. Nine days to get the critical systems secured and the primary habitat inflated.
    57|
    58|She climbed back inside, peeled off her gloves, and sat down at the comm station next to Gabriel.
    59|
    60|"One down," she said quietly. "Twenty-nine to keep alive."
    61|
    62|Mission AI's voice, transmitted privately to her earpiece: "Arun has already begun power‑down sequencing for non‑essential systems. I recommend you get some sleep, Commander. Tomorrow we build."
    63|
    64|She nodded and walked toward her bunk, and the wind outside began its patient work of covering their tracks.
    65|
    66|*End of Chapter 1 — Bridge: The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact.*

    70|## Chapter 2 — Counting What Matters
    71|
    72|*Mission AI: "I am detecting an anomaly in the diagnostic flags for Units R‑7 through R‑12. Recommend immediate inspection of the robotic manipulator arms before load‑bearing operations commence."*
    73|*Jonah Mercer: "On it. Pulling up maintenance logs now."*
    74|
    75|Jonah Mercer was already awake when the pre‑dawn alarm chimed, his boots on the grated floor of the cargo bay, his headlamp cutting a pale cone of light across crate markings and serial numbers. He had been awake for two hours. Could not sleep. The numbers would not stop.
    76|
    77|Forty-seven crates marked priority one. Two hundred and thirty-six items flagged critical for life‑support continuity. One nuclear reactor requiring a seventy‑two‑hour cool‑down before they could even approach the primary coolant connections. And a dust storm to the east that Mission AI projected would reach the landing site in approximately nine days.
    78|
    79|He pulled up the unloading sequence on his tablet. Standard protocol called for three days of cargo triage before any serious construction began. They did not have three days. They had nine before the storm hit, and the storm would coat every solar panel, blind every camera, and clog every seal on the site.
    80|
    81|"Mercer here," he said into his radio. "Running priority triage on critical systems cargo. I need Unit R‑7 through R‑12 cleared for inspection before we start moving anything heavy. Who have I got?"
    82|
    83|"Mei," came the reply. "I'm at the seed vault. Inventory shows nominal temperature on the extremophile strains, but the terrestrial seed packets are running two degrees warm. Nothing fatal yet, but I want to move them to the thermal bus within the hour."
    84|
    85|"Do it. I'll clear the path."
    86|
    87|Jonah pulled on his EVA gloves and stepped into the connecting tunnel between Ship One and Ship Two — the flexible shaft of corrugated aluminum alloy that was, for now, the only thing keeping thirty people from needing suits to talk to each other. The tunnel had been sealed at four points during descent and was holding pressure — barely. A warning indicator at the third seal was blinking amber. He made a note and kept moving.
    88|
    89|Ship Two's cargo bay was a cathedral of crates and machinery. Pressurized habitat modules, still sealed in their launch restraints. Water reclamation units, each one the size of a small car, wrapped in thermal blankets. Solar panel arrays, folded flat like enormous black wings waiting to be unfurled. Greenhouse pallets, heavy with soil analog and irrigation hardware. And everywhere, threaded through the machinery like white thread through a needle, the cables and conduits that would eventually become the colony's nervous system.
    90|
    91|A young technician named Ferreira was standing in the middle of it all, looking slightly overwhelmed. She was twenty‑six, an aerospace engineer from São Paulo, and this was her first deep‑space mission. Her second EVA, ever.
    92|
    93|"Jonah," she said. "The manifest says we have four spare suit bearings in Crate 7‑B. I can't find Crate 7‑B."
    94|
    95|Jonah looked at the bay layout on his tablet. Crate 7‑B was supposed to be in Section 4, forward starboard. It was not there. He walked to the coordinates, ducking under a swing arm from the unloading crane, and found the crate — or what was left of it.
    96|
    97|The landing had shifted it three meters forward and crushed its left side. The impact detector on his tablet pinged: a 4.2‑g deceleration event on final approach. Inside the broken crate, he could see the vacuum‑sealed packets of suit bearings — each one a tiny precision‑machined component worth more, out here, than its weight in gold.
    98|
    99|He opened the crate carefully. Eighteen packets. Four were visibly damaged. The other fourteen appeared intact.
   100|
   101|Ferreira appeared beside him. "Is that—"
   102|
   103|"Fourteen good bearings," Jonah said. "That was the entire spare supply for the first six months. Now it's fourteen. I'm going to bag these and mark them fragile. Nobody touches them without signing for them."
   104|
   105|He sealed the intact packets and tucked them into his tool belt. Something about the moment crystallized for him — the whole gamble of the mission reduced to fourteen vacuum‑sealed packets in a crushed crate. This was what colony meant. Not the grand architecture of settlement. Just fourteen spare parts, and a colony that would live or die by whether those fourteen held.
   106|
   107|On his tablet, he updated the inventory: Suit bearings — critical spares — 14 of 18 intact. He flagged the line in red.
   108|
   109|"Ferreira, pull up the survival‑class breakdown. I want to know exactly what we have in air, water, power, and food before I let anyone sleep tonight."
   110|
   111|Across the ship, Mei Navarro was doing the same thing with seeds. The extremophile strains — engineered to survive extreme cold and drought — were rated for Martian conditions within a tolerance band. The terrestrial seeds, the ones that would eventually provide fresh food rather than just survival rations, were another matter. They needed warmth, water, protection. They needed a greenhouse that did not exist yet.
   112|
   113|She opened the seed vault's thermal blanket and studied the readout. The extremophiles were stable. The terrestrial packets showed 14.2 degrees Celsius — two degrees above optimal. She adjusted the thermal bus connection and watched the number edge down: 14.1, 14.0. Not perfect. But alive.
   114|
   115|Mei was a botanist from Guadalajara, thirty‑four years old, and she had spent six years preparing for this moment. Every model she had built, every growth cycle she had simulated, every argument she had won in conference rooms at mission control — it all came down to fourteen seeds that were currently two degrees too warm in a crate on Mars.
   116|
   117|She touched the vault lid and closed it gently.
   118|
   119|"We'll build you a home," she whispered. "Just give me time."
   120|
   121|In Ship Three, the situation was more complicated. The tilted lander had taken on an awkward geometry that complicated depressurization sequencing, and the crew — three engineers and one pilot — had spent the first six hours running damage assessments instead of unloading. The pilot, Imani Sato, was not worried about the structural integrity of the ship. She was worried about the landing strut that was buried past its midpoint in Martian regolith.
   122|
   123|"If that strut has stress fractures from the tilt," she said over the comm to Elena, "then every load we put on the deck is a load we shouldn't be putting there."
   124|
   125|"Can you assess it visually?"
   126|
   127|"Not completely. I'd need to dig it out. Which means EVA, which means suit time, which I want to spend on cargo."
   128|
   129|Elena studied the feed from Ship Three's external cameras. The strut was angled at nineteen degrees from vertical. It was still holding — Mission AI's structural analysis said it would hold up to a forty‑degree tilt — but the margin was thinner than anyone liked.
   130|
   131|"Log it as a risk," Elena said. "Priority two. We'll deal with it after we get the critical systems out."
   132|
   133|"Copy that," Imani said. "Ship Three out."
   134|
   135|Arun was in the reactor bay, running the Stirling generator through its post‑landing checkout. The machine was a thing of quiet beauty — a heat engine that converted the decay heat of the nuclear core into electricity without any moving parts, its regenerator grids and displacer chambers doing their patient work in a sealed argon atmosphere. Mission AI had sequenced the startup perfectly, as it always did. The generator hummed at 98.7 percent efficiency, producing 34 kilowatts of continuous power that would keep the batteries charged and the life‑support systems running when the dust came.
   136|
   137|"Stirling is online," Arun reported. "We're drawing from the primary solar array for now, but if that storm hits early, the generator will carry the full load."
   138|
   139|"Good," Elena said. "Keep it warm."
   140|
   141|Around the site, the other crews were finishing their initial assessments. Gabriel had documented everything on film — the cracked crate, the tilted ship, the dust already beginning to settle on solar panels and viewports like a slow, patient geological force. He was already thinking about how this day would be remembered. Not as the day they landed. As the day they understood what they had landed in.
   142|
   143|"Gabriel to Elena," he said. "I'm ready to start the founding record if you are."
   144|
   145|Elena looked at the three ships, at the crews moving between them in bulky suits, at the regolith stretching in every direction toward a horizon that offered nothing but distance. She thought about the word foundation — what it meant to build something that would outlast the people who built it.
   146|
   147|"Not yet," she said. "Let's count what we have first."
   148|
   149|*End of Chapter 2 — Bridge: To know what they can survive, they first need a livable base.*

   153|## Chapter 3 — Making Air Between Ships
   154|
   155|*Mission AI: "I am detecting a misalignment of 3.2 millimeters in Seal C‑7 on the primary connecting tunnel between Ship One and Ship Two. Recommend immediate repair before pressurizing the full corridor."*
   156|*Arun Patel: "Mark it. I'll get to it after the airlock test."*
   157|
   158|The connecting tunnel was not a thing of engineering beauty. It was eight meters of flexible aluminum‑alloy shaft, pressure‑rated to hold a human atmosphere but never designed to be elegant about it. Three times during the transit from Earth, the tunnel sections had been tested for micro‑meteorite punctures and pressure seals. Three times they had held. But those tests had been conducted in vacuum, not in the specific Martian conditions of temperature fluctuation and dust intrusion that Mission AI was now tracking in real time.
   159|
   160|Arun floated at the mouth of the tunnel, his toolkit strapped to his thigh, a handheld pressure gauge in his right glove. The amber warning on his cuff display pointed to a coupling seal — a simple collar of aluminum that joined two tunnel sections and held the pressure by way of a rubber O‑ring gasket. The O‑ring was fine. The problem was the flange behind it. During descent, the coupling had shifted 3.2 millimeters off center, and that shift meant the seal was being asked to do work it was not designed to do.
   161|
   162|He pulled the access panel and studied the flange. It was bent — not catastrophically, but enough that re‑aligning it would require prying it back into position with a lever bar, then re‑torquing the bolts. Simple work, if you had gravity. In micro‑gravity, with a pressure differential already building on the other side, it required a particular kind of focus.
   163|
   164|"Arun," Elena's voice came through his earpiece. "How's the tunnel?"
   165|
   166|"Three millimeters off. I'm going to try to re‑set the flange."
   167|
   168|"If it blows, you'll lose pressure in both ships."
   169|
   170|"I know."
   171|
   172|He found a flat head on his pry bar and seated it against the bent flange. Braced his feet against the tunnel wall, steadied himself in the micro‑gravity, and pushed. The metal groaned. Shifted. Groaned again. He pushed harder, feeling the cold of the bar through his glove, and the flange moved — a fraction of a millimeter at first, then a sudden, clean clunk as it seated back into alignment.
   173|
   174|"Got it," he said. "Passing the bolts."
   175|
   176|Behind him, through the open hatch into Ship Two's habitat module, Gabriel was watching. He had his tablet recording, as he always did, but he was also just watching. The image of Arun's boots braced against the wall of the tunnel, working a piece of bent metal back into place, was the image Gabriel knew he would use someday when he explained to someone — a journalist, a historian, a child in a schoolroom — what it actually looked like to build a colony. It did not look like construction cranes or grand openings. It looked like one man in a bulky suit, working a pry bar in a cramped space, fixing a three‑millimeter problem that could have killed everyone.
   177|
   178|Arun finished re‑torquing the bolts, installed a secondary clamp over the coupling as a backup, and ran the pressure test again. Seal C‑7: green. Full corridor pressurization holding at 101.3 kilopascals.
   179|
   180|"Tunnel is go," he reported.
   181|
   182|Elena's voice came back: "Copy. Proceed with the rest of the connecting sequence."
   183|
   184|The procedure called for three tunnel connections: Ship One to Ship Two (complete), Ship Two to Ship Three (pending, complicated by Ship Three's tilt), and Ship One to the primary habitat module (the inflatable structure that would serve as the colony's first communal living space, scheduled for deployment in forty‑eight hours). One by one, the connections would turn three isolated vessels into a single pressure envelope — a bubble of borrowed Earth atmosphere on a planet that wanted nothing to do with human lungs.
   185|
   186|Imani Sato was leading the Ship Two to Ship Three connection, and the tilt was making everything harder. The geometry of the link required a custom‑bent transition section that Jonah was fabricating in the Ship Two workshop — a job that should have taken six hours was stretching toward eight as Jonah worked through miscalculated load tolerances and a drill bit that skipped twice on the aluminum.
   187|
   188|Jonah did not complain. He cut, tested, measured, and recut. The transition section was a piece of bent metal, but it was also the collar that would connect one life to another. He tested it three times before he let Imani take it.
   189|
   190|"Hang on," he said over the comm, handing the piece to the robot arm that would ferry it across the gap between ships. "One more torque check."
   191|
   192|"You've already checked it four times."
   193|
   194|"And you'll be glad I checked it a fifth."
   195|
   196|The transition section moved across the gap on the robot arm, guided by Imani's remote control and Mission AI's real‑time spatial calibration. The distance between the two airlocks was exactly 4.7 meters. The transition piece was 4.65 meters. The margin was five centimeters — acceptable, if everything went perfectly, which it never did on Mars.
   197|
   198|It went perfectly. The section seated. The seals engaged. Imani ran the pressure test, watching the gauge climb from vacuum to 50 kilopascals, then 80, then 101.3.
   199|
   200|"Tunnel Two is go," she reported.
   201|
   202|Elena acknowledged. "That's two of three. One to go."
   203|
   204|The mood in the mess hall that evening was different from the mood in the morning. In the morning, it had been sharp with adrenaline — the raw electricity of survival, of three ships that had made it to the surface. Now it was something quieter. More careful. The first meals were being served from rehydrated pouches, eaten in silence, everyone processing the same unspoken fact: they were here, they were alive, and tomorrow the real work started.
   205|
   206|Gabriel sat at the end of a bench, his tablet dark beside him, and listened. Tomas Hale was explaining to a junior crew member why robotics was going to be the most important discipline on Mars — not engineering or medicine, but robotics — because thirty people could not build a city without tireless, accurate, obedient machine labor to multiply every decision and every action. The junior crew member was nodding, skeptical but willing to be convinced.
   207|
   208|Laila Okonkwo sat across from Mei, the two of them sharing a silence that was comfortable. Mei was studying a seed packet on her tablet — germination timelines, optimal growth temperatures, water requirements. She was already planning the greenhouse, already calculating how many calories of fresh food the colony could produce in six months, twelve months, two years. The numbers were not encouraging yet. But they were a start.
   209|
   210|Through the viewport, Ship Three's running lights blinked amber against the darkening sky. The dust storm to the east had slowed its advance — Mission AI's latest projection gave them an extra eighteen hours before the first particles reached the site. It was not a reprieve. It was a warning.
   211|
   212|Arun returned from the tunnel and dropped into a seat, his coveralls dusty, his hands showing the faint red marks of tool work. Elena was already at the comm station, reviewing tomorrow's EVA assignments. The priority list had changed since that morning. The connecting tunnels were done. Now it was about the solar arrays, the reactor, the habitat module, and — underneath everything — the clock that Mission AI kept quietly ticking in every terminal.
   213|
   214|"Tomorrow we start building a home," Mission AI said, its voice filling the room from the central speaker. "I recommend nine hours of sleep. You will need it."
   215|

   222|## Chapter 4 — The Last Normal Messages
   223|
   224|*Mission AI: "The next scheduled transmission window from Earth arrives in 4 hours, 17 minutes. Current packet queue shows 23 incoming messages for crew. I recommend reviewing priority flags before distribution."*

   226|
   227|The communications array on Ship One was not designed for this.    232|

   238|

   240|
   241|The messages from family and friends were the ones Gabriel was trying not to read. Personal transmissions were supposed to be sacred — the private threads that connected the crew to the people who loved them. But the operational flags on some of them were hard to ignore: priority reroutes, subject matter changes, language that had been edited between the version the sender had written and the version the crew was receiving.

   243|One message, from Elena's husband in Ann Arbor, had arrived stripped of its subject line and much of its body text.    245|Gabriel held the message and did not deliver it. Not yet. Not until he knew what the operational picture actually was, and what Elena was going to tell the crew about it.
   246|
   247|He called Mission AI on the private channel. "AI, give me an honest assessment. What's happening on Earth?"
   248|

   251|"Gabriel, I have processed 4,200 incoming transmissions in the last eighteen hours. The majority are operational re‑routes and priority escalations.    253|Gabriel absorbed this. "Is anyone coming to get us?"
   254|
   255|"That question cannot be answered with current data. The operational messages I am receiving do not contain a rescue plan, a return timeline, or a resource commitment. They contain a request that we continue to operate autonomously and await further instruction."

   257|"How long can we wait?"

   259|"With current supplies and the equipment on site: indefinitely, if we are careful. The more precise answer depends on how quickly we can establish local food production and water extraction.    265|"Understood, Gabriel."

   267|The mess hall that evening was its usual self. Rehydrated stew, already eaten mostly in silence, the conversations winding down toward sleep. Elena sat at the comm station reviewing the operational messages Gabriel had flagged, her face unreadable in the blue glow of the screen.
   268|

   291|## Chapter 5 — Two-Year Thinking
   292|
   293|*Mission AI: "I am detecting an anomaly in the mission timeline data. The projected return window has shifted from Sol 720 to Sol 1080 without an associated mission directive. Recommend clarification from Earth. I will continue to flag this in all future communications."*
   294|*Elena Varga: "Noted. Keep flagging it."*
   295|
   296|The mission timeline was stored in Mission AI's memory banks as a sequence of numbered sol events — Sol 0 for landing, Sol 720 for the scheduled departure window, Sol 730 for Earth return. The logic was simple and brutal: two years on Mars, then home. Everything from food packaging to suit rotation schedules had been built around that assumption. The return ship — the vessel that would carry thirty people back to orbit, where the homeward fleet would be waiting — was a separate spacecraft that would arrive at Mars orbit six months before the crew was scheduled to leave the surface.
   297|
   298|Except the timeline had shifted. Arun had noticed it first, running the orbital mechanics models during the transit, when Mission AI had flagged a trajectory adjustment that did not match any directive in the mission plan. He had recalculated three times before he came to Elena with it.
   299|
   300|"The return window is off by three hundred and sixty sols," he said. They were sitting in the small conference space that served as Ship One's command briefing room. The door was closed. "That's a year. Not three months. A year."
   301|

More power. More everything.
   303|
   304|"Can we make a year?" she asked.
   305|

   307|
   308|"And we can't reduce caloric consumption by eighteen percent and do the work we're here to do."
   309|
   310|"No."
   311|
   312|She studied the orbital diagram.    313|
   314|She thought about calling a crew meeting. She thought about the look on thirty faces when she told them the return date was a year later than expected.    315|
   316|She thought about it for a long time. Then she closed the file and went back to the EVA schedule.
   317|
   318|Not yet. Not until she had numbers she could actually defend.
   319|
   320|Three days later, she had the numbers. They were worse than she had expected.
   321|
   322|The food shortage was real but manageable — Mei's greenhouse could supplement the packaged diet enough to close the gap, if the first crops grew on schedule. The dust storm that was now coating every solar panel on the site had reduced power generation by 31 percent, which meant the batteries were running down faster than the charging cycle could replenish them.    323|
   324|Arun's solution was to reduce the colony's operational footprint. Run the water extraction during daylight hours when the solar contribution was highest. Shut down the atmospheric processors during the early morning and late evening, when temperature differentials placed the heaviest load on the thermal management system. Stagger the greenhouse lighting cycles so that only half the growing area was under artificial light at any given time.
   325|
   326|It was not elegant. It was not even safe, by the standards of the original mission plan. But it would keep the colony alive until the dust settled and the solar arrays could be cleaned.
   327|
   328|"It's the math," Arun said to Elena and Gabriel in the command briefing room. "I can make it work for twelve months if — and this is a very large if — nothing catastrophic happens.    329|
   330|"And if the math breaks?"
   331|
   332|"Then we start making harder choices."
   333|
   334|Gabriel had been listening without speaking. He was thinking about what Mission AI had told him in the communications bay — the possibility that no one was coming at all, not in three hundred sixty sols, not ever. He had not shared that with Elena yet. He was not sure he should.
   335|
   336|"AI," he said, looking at the ceiling speaker. "Realistically. What's the chance Earth sends a rescue mission if we're not able to get back on the original schedule?"
   337|
   338|Mission AI's pause was even longer this time. "I cannot assign a probability to that question with any confidence. What I can say is that in the 4,200 transmissions I have processed in the last thirty days, I have found no reference to a rescue plan, a recovery mission, or an emergency evacuation protocol for the Ares‑One crew.    339|
   340|The room was quiet. The hum of the life support system was the loudest sound in it.

   342|"Okay," Elena said. She stood up, folded her tablet under her arm, and looked at Arun and Gabriel with the expression of someone who had just finished a long and difficult diagnosis.    343|
   344|She paused at the door. "And Gabriel — keep analyzing those transmissions. If that picture changes, I want to know before anyone else does."
   345|
   346|"Understood," Gabriel said.
   347|
   348|She left. Arun followed.
   349|
   350|Gabriel sat alone in the briefing room for a moment, thinking about what Elena had just said. Acting like a colony. It was a phrase that shifted everything and nothing at the same time. A colony was not a visit. A colony was a commitment. A colony was a place you planned to stay in, and planned to stay in permanently, with the full knowledge that the people who sent you might never come back.
   351|
   352|He opened a new file on his tablet and titled it: *Ares‑One Founding Record — Day 14*.
   353|
   354|He began to type.

# Chapter 11 – False Ice

The convoy crawled into the airlock bay at 1417 hours local time, twelve hours earlier than scheduled. Nobody cheered. The hatches opened and the crew came out moving like people who had been holding bad news too long.

Gabriel watched them from the inner door of the pressure tunnel. Imani was last out of the lead rover. She pulled her helmet off and stood there with her eyes closed, not saying anything, just breathing recycled air that smelled like other people's sweat and machine oil. That told him everything.

The drill team had left at dawn the previous day with four rovers, two heavy drills, a melting rig, and seven people. They came back with three rovers—one had thrown a traction belt on bad ground and they'd abandoned it—one drill core in a sample tube that should have been full of ice, and a silence that spread through the base faster than any announcement.

Jonah was the first to speak. He had come up from the workshop crusted with cutting fluid and metal dust, and he stood at the edge of the staging area with his arms crossed, reading the body language of the returning crew like a fault code.

"That's it?" he said. "One tube?"

Imani opened her eyes. "That's what came up."

"Fourteen hours of drilling, two hundred kilometers of driving, and you brought back a sample you could fit in your pocket."

"I know what we brought back, Jonah."

"Then tell me what happened."

The staging area went quiet. People stopped and turned. Gabriel felt the familiar tension—the kind that came when tired people needed someone to blame.

Imani set her helmet on the rover hood with deliberate care. "The ground signatures looked right. Every spectral pass before departure showed consistent hydrogen returns. TIR anomaly matched what we'd expect from a shallow ice lens. We drilled to fifteen meters and pulled nothing but dry regolith with trace hydration. Secondary target, twenty-two meters, same result. The tool returns looked like ice. They felt like ice. But the ground didn't deliver."

"The ground doesn't lie," Jonah said.

"The ground tells the truth in a language we're still learning to read." Imani's voice was flat. Controlled. "We read the phonetics wrong."

Mei stepped forward from the crowd gathered at the mess entrance. "What was the actual water content?"

"On the primary core? 0.4 percent by mass. Bound hydration. Not extractable with our current energy budget without cooking the entire column."

"Then we can't use it."

"No shit," Jonah said. "That's the point. We burned seventy hours of collective EVA time, wrote off a rover we can't replace, consumed power we don't have to spare, and came back with a geological curiosity." He turned and pointed a finger at the ceiling, which was the direction of the surface. "We landed in the wrong place."

"Aldrin chose this site," Elena said.

She had entered from Command without anyone noticing. She stood in the shadow of the structural column near the rear pressure door, arms at her sides, voice calm in a way that made people pay attention precisely because it was so measured.

"Aldrin chose it based on the best remote sensing data available from orbital reconnaissance," she continued. "Every survey, every lander mission, every radar pass for thirty years pointed to this region as the most water-rich landing zone in the northern lowlands. The decision wasn't a guess. It was the product of every space agency on Earth."

"Then Earth was wrong," Jonah said.

"Earth was working with satellite data from Mars orbit." Imani's voice carried an edge now. "Satellites see the top meter. Sometimes two, if the ground is dry enough. We're looking for ice at ten, fifteen, thirty meters. That's not a measurement error. That's a limitation of the whole approach."

"So what's your excuse?"

"I'm not making an excuse. I'm telling you what the science says. The hydrogen returns were real. The thermal signatures were real. But the interpretation was wrong. We thought it meant massive shallow ice. It meant trace hydration in a deep dry layer with a false thermal profile. The data didn't lie—we just read it wrong."

Gabriel watched Elena's face. She was letting the argument run because she needed to see who would fracture first. That was how she worked. She didn't step into every fire. Sometimes she let the fire expose the weak points in the crew and only then brought the extinguisher.

The weak points were showing.

Hiroshi, the youngest of the drill crew, sat on a supply crate with his head down. He had been on Mars for three months and he looked like a man who had just realized the planet was bigger than his training. A woman from Life Support—Gabriel thought her name was Chen—stood near the greenhouse entrance with her arms wrapped around herself, the universal posture of someone who had done the math on how long the base could last without new water.

Elena let it run another fifteen seconds. Then she stepped into the center of the staging area.

"Enough."

She didn't shout. The word carried anyway.

"We are not having the 'wrong landing site' conversation. That's not a decision tree with useful branches. We're here. The ships are here. The equipment is here. The only question that matters is what we do from this position."

"We need water," Jonah said.

"I'm aware of what we need."

"Then don't tell me we're not—"

"I'm not telling you anything except what's productive." Elena's voice hardened. "Blame doesn't extract ice. Recrimination doesn't fill a single tank. I've seen exactly what happens to small teams under pressure when they start eating each other, and it doesn't end with more water. It ends with people making worse decisions because they're too busy being right at each other to be right about the problem."

She turned to Imani. "What's your assessment?"

"The site we chose has ice. Just not accessible ice. The bound water is real but uneconomical. We'd spend more energy extracting it than we'd recover, which makes the whole exercise thermodynamically stupid. But this region has more varied terrain than our initial surveys covered. We hit two targets. There are at least six more within range, plus three deeper anomaly clusters that the orbital data flagged but we didn't prioritize because the shallow stuff looked easier."

"Priorities were wrong."

"Yes. We chased the easy signature. We should chase the deep one."

"Range?"

"Hundred and forty kilometers northeast. The terrain is worse—rougher ground, more elevation change, probably slower travel speeds. But the signatures are stronger and deeper. If the deep model is right, there's a buried lens at thirty-five to forty meters that could be massive. Possibly hundreds of millions of cubic meters of accessible ice."

"Possibly?"

"Orbital data can't confirm thickness from that depth. It sees a density anomaly with the right dielectric properties. It could be pure ice. It could be dirty ice. It could be something else entirely that happens to look like ice in the sensor bands we used."

"So another gamble."

"Every drill hole is a gamble. The question is whether the odds are better than the last bet."

Elena was quiet for a moment. The air handlers hummed. A pump cycled somewhere in the walls. Gabriel counted the seconds—nine of them—before she spoke again.

"We expand the survey. Imani, you pick the three most promising deep targets from the existing data. We'll run a ground-penetrating radar transect to each one before we commit another full drilling operation. That costs time but saves the kind of failure we just had."

"Ground radar adds four days per transect," Imani said. "Minimum."

"I know."

"And we still have the problem that GPR can tell us there's something there, but it can't guarantee purity or access until we put a drill string into it."

"Then we'll have better data to decide which hole we take the risk on. Plan the first transect. Start tomorrow."

Imani nodded. The tension in her shoulders didn't drop, but something in her eyes shifted from defensive to focused. She had a task now, and tasks were easier to carry than blame.

The staging area began to break up. People drifted back to their stations. Jonah didn't move.

"I need the robots," he said.

Elena turned. "What robots?"

"The prospecting units. Imani took four on the last run. Two didn't come back. That's three left. I need them for habitat expansion. We're still sleeping in three shifts because we don't have enough enclosed volume, and we're losing work hours we can't afford."

"The robots are assigned to survey operations," Tomas said. He had appeared from the robot control alcove, tablet in hand, voice carrying the particular precision of someone who had already run the numbers. "That allocation was approved."

"It was approved before the survey turned up nothing."

"The failure of one survey doesn't invalidate the allocation."

"It means we wasted resources we could have used building." Jonah's voice was rising. "I've got pressure shell sections in the cargo bay. Each section weighs three hundred kilos. I can move them with the sled, but I need robots to position and seal them. Without that, we're looking at manual handling—four people and six hours per section. We have eleven sections. That's two hundred and sixty-four man-hours I don't have."

Tomas didn't look up. "The robots are running survey support. Survey support is water search. Water search is the priority."

"Water search came back empty."

"Water search came back with data. The next search has better targets. Canceling robot support now to save labor on habitat expansion creates a scenario where we have more volume but no water to fill a single tank. That's a faster death than sleeping in shifts."

Jonah took a step toward Tomas. He was bigger than the robot engineer, and the movement was not lost on anyone.

"You want to run that math again?"

"I already ran it. I can show you the curves. At current consumption, with recycling at 92 percent and accounting for unavoidable losses, we have 147 days of usable water. Expanding volume adds 3 percent to daily consumption. Adding a second greenhouse adds 12 percent. Without new extraction within 90 days, we enter critical shortage. Habitable volume becomes irrelevant. You can't fill a larger house without water."

"You're telling me my job doesn't matter."

"I'm telling you building comes after survival. That's not personal. It's resource sequencing. If you want to argue with the math, argue with the math. But the math doesn't care about your feelings."

"Tomas," Elena said. A warning.

"I'm being accurate."

"You're being accurate in a way that escalates."

"Would you prefer I be inaccurate?"

Elena held his gaze. Tomas held it back. He wasn't challenging her—Gabriel had learned to read the difference. Tomas simply did not recognize emotional arguments as valid inputs to optimization problems. It wasn't a character flaw. It was a limitation of his operating system, and on some days it was useful and on other days it made everyone want to throw him out an airlock.

"Reassign two robots to Jonah," Elena said. "Temporarily. He gets them for forty-eight hours to get the first four pressure sections assembled. After that, they return to survey support."

"Forty-eight hours isn't enough," Jonah said.

"Then you'll have to prioritize. Get the sections that matter most done first."

"Every section matters."

"Then make them matter in order." Elena's voice had the finality of a sealed hatch. "Jonah, you get two robots for two days. Imani, you plan the ground radar transects with three robots instead of four. Work around it. I know both of you can, because if you couldn't, you wouldn't have been selected for this mission."

She walked away before anyone could argue further. That was her signature—she didn't stay for the dying echoes of a decision. She made it and moved on, leaving the people who didn't like it to choke on their objections in private.

Gabriel found Mei in the greenhouse ten minutes later. She was inspecting a tray of bean seedlings with the kind of attention that was really about avoiding other thoughts. The grow lights cast a pinkish-purple glow across her face that made her look tired in a way that went deeper than sleep debt.

"Tough day," he said.

She didn't look up. "Is there any other kind?"

"Fair point."

He pulled a stool from under the workbench and sat down. The greenhouse was the warmest part of the base, always a few degrees above the main corridor temperature, and the air was thick with the smell of damp soil and green growth. It was the closest thing to Earth they had left.

"Can I ask you something?"

"You're going to anyway."

"The drill team did everything right, didn't they?"

Mei's hands stopped moving. She straightened and looked at him with an expression that was half amusement, half something sharper.

"Yes. That's the part nobody wants to say out loud."

"Why not?"

"Because it's scarier than incompetence. If they'd made a mistake—if Imani had read the data wrong, if the drill crew had missed a target that was obvious in retrospect—we could fix that. We could train better. Write better procedures. Buy better sensors. The problem would be in our control." She turned back to the seedlings. "But they didn't make a mistake. They did excellent science on excellent data and got a result that's useless for survival. That's the difference between research and colonialism. Research celebrates negative results. Negative results are data. They refine the model. They make the next experiment smarter."

"And colonialism?"

"Colonialism needs water. It doesn't care whether the data that misled us was beautifully collected. It doesn't care about publication. It doesn't care about the refinement of our geological understanding of the Martian northern lowlands. It cares about one thing: whether we can extract the resource we need before the reserve runs dry. Good science can still produce bad outcomes when the question is survival. Because survival doesn't grade on a curve. The planet doesn't reward you for having the right methods. It rewards you for being right."

Gabriel sat with that for a moment. The grow lights hummed.

"You sound like you've thought about this before."

"I've thought about nothing else since I saw the crop yield projections on day three." Mei touched a seedling leaf. "I can grow the most efficient plants ever cultivated in a closed system. I can write papers that will be cited for decades. And if the water runs out, none of it matters. The plants die. We die. The papers rot in an archive nobody will ever read."

"That's a cheerful thought."

"I'm a biologist. I deal in truths that don't care about morale."

She looked at him directly. Her eyes held something hard—a stubborn clarity that had made its peace with the odds without accepting the outcome.

"The good news," she said, "is that we're not wrong about everything. The ice exists. The data was telling the truth about hydrogen. We just didn't understand the grammar. Next time we might."

"Next time we have to."

"Yes."

Gabriel left her to her seedlings and walked back through the main corridor. Ship Two's interior had become the central spine of the colony—the place where people passed, where conversations happened, where the board on the wall tracked every critical resource in the settlement. He stopped to read it.

**WATER**

Import reserves: 12,740 liters

Recycling rate: 92.3 percent

Effective endurance: 147 days at current consumption

Projected endurance with extraction failure: 134 days (accounts for degradation)

Status: YELLOW

Below the main board, in Imani's handwriting on the whiteboard underneath, someone had added a note in red marker:

"Every liter we export for drilling is a liter we don't drink. Every liter we find is a liter we get to use twice."

Gabriel stared at the numbers. One hundred forty-seven days. Five months. That was their runway. After that, the air would start getting thin in a different way.

He walked to the Command module. Elena was alone, sitting at her console with a tablet. She didn't look up when Gabriel entered, but she shifted slightly, acknowledging him without words.

"How bad is it really?" he asked.

"Bad enough that I'm not going to pretend." She set the tablet down. "Jonah is right about more volume. Mei is right about more greenhouse. Tomas is right that the robots are the bottleneck for everything. Imani is right that the ice exists somewhere. Everyone is right, and everyone's rightness conflicts, and my job is to figure out whose rightness gets to kill us slowest if we bet on the wrong answer."

"That's a hell of a job description."

"It's the only one that matters on Mars." She rubbed her eyes. "The deep survey is the right move. But it's a bet. If the ice isn't there, we start talking about what a hundred-thirty-four-day survival plan looks like. And that conversation doesn't end well."

"You think the ice is there."

"I think the ice has to be there. That's not analysis. That's hope wearing a data coat."

Gabriel sat down across from her. "I want to document the next survey. Not just the science. The crew. What happens when people are stretched this thin."

Elena looked at him for a long moment. "You want to write the obituary before the death."

"No. I want to write the evidence that we were alive while we were trying."

That got something from her. A small shift at the corner of her mouth. Not quite a smile, but close.

"Fine. But you stay out of the way. If Imani has to pull you out of a ditch, I'll lock you in the archive until the ice runs out."

"Fair."

The next forty-eight hours were a controlled collision.

Jonah took his two robots and worked sixteen-hour shifts assembling pressure sections. He slept in the workshop—Gabriel saw a sleeping bag unrolled on the floor next to the welding station—and he drove the robots with a single-mindedness that bordered on obsession. By the end of the second day, four new berthing modules were connected and pressurized. The base's usable volume increased by 22 percent. People slept better that night. Even the food tasted different, or maybe that was just the relief of having space.

But the cost was visible. Two robots that could have been surveying ground were hauling wall panels. Three days of survey time lost while the colony got more comfortable. Comfort that wouldn't matter if the next drill came up dry.

Imani ran her transects with the remaining three robots, working around the clock with a crew of four. The ground radar went out on the third day and came back with data that made her sit down in the middle of the staging area and stare at the display for a full minute without speaking.

Gabriel found her there.

"What is it?"

She looked up at him with an expression he couldn't read. Then she turned the screen toward him.

The radar profile showed a massive dielectric anomaly at thirty-eight meters depth. The signature was clean. Deep. Uniform. The kind of signal that textbooks used as examples of what a buried ice lens looked like on a ground-penetrating radar cross-section.

"Is it real?" he asked.

"I don't know." Imani's voice was steady, but there was something underneath it. A wire pulled tight. "It looks real. It looks exactly like what we wanted to see. That's what the last signature looked like too."

"Then how do you know?"

She stared at the screen. The lines of the radar profile were sharp and clear. They showed something underground that could save the colony or destroy it.

"I don't," she said.

She stood up and closed the display.

"Tell Elena we're going back out. Tomorrow. Full convoy, full drill, full extraction rig. If this is ice, we bring it home. If it's false ice, we find out now, because we don't have time to run another survey."

Gabriel nodded.

"One more thing," she said.

"What?"

"Pack for a week. If this one's empty, I'm not coming back until we find something that isn't."

She walked away before he could answer.

Gabriel stood in the empty staging area, looking at the hatch that led to the surface. Outside, Mars was waiting. The same planet that had fooled them once, with the same tricks, the same sky, the same dust.

They would go out again because the alternative was staying in and watching the numbers count down.

They would go out knowing the data could be beautiful and wrong.

They would go out with fewer illusions and exactly the same hope, because hope was the only fuel they had left that hadn't been rationed yet.

*End of Chapter 11*
